steps.user_message: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm married filing jointly in Boston MA. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $12,500 in 1099 income (IT contracting, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2016–2020). I donated $1,400 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $890 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — here’s a clear overview based on your details for 2023 (married filing jointly, Boston MA).

What you can deduct (federal)
- Standard vs itemizing
  - Standard deduction (MFJ, 2023): $27,700.
  - Your likely itemized deductions are limited (no mortgage, you rent). Rough estimate:
    - State income tax (SALT) around ~5% of W‑2 wages ≈ ~$3,200 (cap is $10,000, but you’re far below).
    - Charitable gifts: $1,400.
    - Total likely itemized ≈ ~$4,600 — far below $27,700. So take the standard deduction.

- Above-the-line deductions (reduce AGI even if you take standard)
  - Student loan interest: Up to $2,500 (you paid $3,600; income is well under the MFJ phase-out). Deduct $2,500 on Schedule 1.
  - Half of self-employment tax: Deductible on Schedule 1 after it’s computed on Schedule SE.

- Self-employment (1099) income and expenses
  - Report $12,500 gross on Schedule C.
  - Deduct ordinary/necessary business expenses. Your $890 of “work expenses”:
    - If related to 1099 contracting: deduct on Schedule C.
    - If for your W‑2 job: not deductible for 2023.
  - Home office (used exclusively and regularly for the 1099 work):
    - Simplified method: 140 sq ft × $5 = $700.
    - Regular method: allocate rent by business-use percentage = 140/620 ≈ 22.6%; annual rent $28,800 → about $6,500 potentially deductible (plus a share of utilities/insurance if applicable). The regular method requires good records and can’t create/increase a Schedule C loss; excess carries forward.
    - Choose the method that yields the best allowed deduction and fits your recordkeeping.
  - Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: Likely eligible for up to 20% of your Schedule C profit (Form 8995), given your income level.

- Investment and interest income
  - $1,450 from Marcus = 1099-INT (report as interest).
  - $320 from TD Ameritrade:
    - If dividends (1099-DIV): report as dividends; Schedule B only if ordinary dividends > $1,500.
    - If sales/gains (1099-B): report on Form 8949/Schedule D.
  - Schedule B is required only if interest > $1,500 or ordinary dividends > $1,500 or certain other conditions. With $1,450 interest and $320 dividends, you typically don’t need it (unless there are other accounts).

Forms you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040.
- Schedule 1 (student loan interest; half SE tax).
- Schedule C (self-employment income/expenses).
- Schedule SE (self-employment tax).
- Form 8829 if you use the regular home office method; not needed if you use the simplified method (report directly on Schedule C).
- Form 8995 (QBI deduction) if you have positive Schedule C profit.
- Schedule B only if required (see above).
- Schedule D/Form 8949 if you sold investments.

Massachusetts notes (not tax advice, just a heads-up)
- MA Form 1 plus any applicable schedules.
- MA offers a renter’s deduction (up to a capped amount; increased in recent law changes) — worth claiming given your rent. Keep your lease and payment records.

Bottom line
- Take the federal standard deduction ($27,700).
- Deduct:
  - Up to $2,500 student loan interest.
  - Schedule C expenses (include home office and any 1099-related costs).
  - Half of SE tax (auto-calculated).
  - Likely a QBI deduction on your net business income.

Open items to confirm
- Is the $890 of “work expenses” tied to your 1099 contracting (so we’ll put it on Schedule C) or to your W‑2 job (not deductible)?
- Was the $320 from TD Ameritrade dividends or realized gains from sales?

If you share those two details, I can refine the deduction amounts and your form list precisely.
